title: Does Romans 13 Mean Christians Must Obey Every Government?
subtitle: Paul told a small church in Nero's Rome to submit to rulers he called God's servants. What that meant for them, what it asks now, and why it never meant obeying every order.

sections.title: Quoted From Pulpits and Podiums
sections.body:
Few people frame Romans 13:1 or write it inside a graduation card. Most of us meet it in an argument. It's read from pulpits before elections, quoted from podiums to defend policies, and pasted into comment threads under news of a protest. In the Berean Standard Bible it reads: “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God” (Romans 13:1).

It's loved as well, and for good reasons. Anyone who has lived where the law stopped working knows that order is a mercy, and that its absence falls hardest on the weak. The Christian who wears a badge or sits on the bench hears in it that such work can be service to God. And the believer weary of the contempt in our politics hears something steadier: the people who govern, including the ones he voted against, are owed more than scorn. None of these readers is wrong. They are hearing Paul.

The skeptic has a case too, and it should be granted in full. This chapter has been used to demand obedience to regimes that deserved none, and church leaders did much of the demanding. In 1850 Northern preachers cited it to make obeying the Fugitive Slave Act a Christian duty. In the 1930s German church leaders used it to call believers to loyalty to Hitler's state. In 1985 South African theologians, in the Kairos Document, exposed the apartheid state's use of this passage to claim absolute and divine authority. The skeptic notices that the verse tends to be quoted by those who hold power at those who don't. Christians supplied most of his evidence, and pastors more than our share.

What answers him, and what the verse's friends need too, is the chapter Paul wrote.

sections.title: A Letter to Christians Under Nero
sections.body:
Paul wrote Romans to house churches of Jewish and Gentile believers in a city he had not yet visited (Romans 1:13). The letter is commonly dated to the mid-50s AD, early in Nero's reign and years before he turned on the church. Some of its readers already knew what an imperial order could do. Not long before, “Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome” (Acts 18:2), and Priscilla and Aquila, driven out by the edict, were back with a church in their house when Paul wrote (Romans 16:3-5).

Chapter numbers came more than a thousand years later; Paul's paragraph on the authorities runs straight on from the one before it. Romans 12 closes with commands for living among people who wish you harm: “Bless those who persecute you” (12:14), “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (12:19), and “overcome evil with good” (12:21). Then come the authorities, appointed by God (13:1): the ruler is “God’s servant for your good” and “does not carry the sword in vain” (13:4), and is owed taxes, respect, and honor (13:6-7). The Greek ties the two paragraphs together. When Paul calls the ruler “an agent of retribution” (13:4), he uses a word from the same family as the vengeance the believers were just told to renounce, and the wrath they were to leave room for in 12:19 is the word the BSB renders as punishment in 13:5. The vengeance the church lays down isn't abolished. God keeps it, and for now some of it passes through a magistrate's hands.

Right after the paragraph, Paul changes the kind of debt. “Pay everyone what you owe him” (13:7) gives way to “Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love” (13:8), a debt nobody finishes paying, since love of neighbor fulfills the whole law (13:9-10). Then he looks at the clock: “The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near” (13:12). The authorities serve inside a night that is ending, and the church is told to dress for the day: “clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ” (13:14).

sections.title: Borrowed Authority
sections.body:
To a small church in the capital, the chapter cut two ways. It told them to submit. A community without standing might have met Rome's power with contempt, or heard in the confession that Jesus is Lord a summons to throw it off. Paul closes both doors. They are to pay what they owe (13:7), and his Greek verb for pay is the one Jesus used when he said, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Mark 12:17).

It also put Caesar in his place. In an empire that offered worship to its emperors, Paul says there is no authority except from God, which makes Nero's authority borrowed, and the lender is Israel's God. Through Jeremiah, God called the king of Babylon “My servant Nebuchadnezzar” (Jeremiah 27:6), yet Daniel's friends refused to worship his statue, and Daniel, announcing God's judgment on the king's pride, told him that “the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes” (Daniel 4:25). A servant of God is never beyond God's judgment. Paul's word for servant in Romans 13:4 is the one he uses for Christ, who “has become a servant of the circumcised” (Romans 15:8), and for Phoebe, “a servant of the church in Cenchrea” (16:1). It names a job: to be a terror to bad conduct rather than good (13:3), serving God “for your good” (13:4).

So the command carried a promise. The power over them was not the last power, God had not left evil unrestrained, and the night was nearly over. They would need every word of it. Within a decade Nero blamed Rome's Christians for the fire of AD 64 and put many of them to death, and early tradition holds that Paul himself was executed under Nero. For generations afterward, Christians paid their taxes and prayed for emperors, and some of them died rather than worship one.

sections.title: What It Asks, and What It Never Said
sections.body:
We don't live under Nero, but the principle reaches us intact. Authority is real, it comes from God, and it exists for the good of the governed. Christians aren't revolutionaries by default: we owe taxes and honor, and prayer “for kings and all those in authority” (1 Timothy 2:2). The promise holds too. No government has the last word.

What the verse doesn't teach is that every command must be obeyed, or that the state is beyond judgment. The same Bible has the apostles telling the council that forbade them to preach, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), then preaching on after being flogged (5:40-42). It has three officials of Babylon who would not “worship the golden statue you have set up” (Daniel 3:18), and Daniel praying at his open window against the king's decree, then telling him, “I have done no wrong against you” (6:22). None of them took up arms, and none of them obeyed. Revelation goes further: “the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne” (Revelation 13:2), and the beast demands worship and makes war on the saints. However that beast is read, Scripture knows a government can stop serving God and claim his place. A skeptic who thinks the Bible blesses whoever holds power has to explain why so many of its heroes ended up in a furnace, a lions' den, or a cell.

Today's misreading runs in both political directions. The Christian on the right who reads Romans 13 aloud when his party governs and finds the beast in the other party's first executive order is making the same move as the Christian on the left who does the reverse. Each has real reasons to fear what the other would do with power. James Davison Hunter has argued that the Christian Right and Left share two things: an assumption that the state is the main instrument for changing the world, and a politics of grievance that turns opponents into enemies. Once the state matters that much, whoever holds it becomes God's servant or the beast. I feel that pull myself, and I'm a pastor, charged with preaching the whole chapter to both halves of the room. Romans 13 doesn't change sides when the government does.

sections.title: Honor Without Worship
sections.body:
Living the verse begins with the ordinary things it asks. Pay your taxes honestly. Speak of officials the way you'd want to be spoken of in their place, and pray for them by name. First Peter puts the posture in one line: “fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17). The fear belongs to God alone; the honor goes to whoever holds the office.

Submission isn't servility. Paul himself made the magistrates of Philippi come and escort him out of jail after they beat Roman citizens without a trial (Acts 16:37-39). Using the law and holding officials to it honors the authority God has set in place, and in a democracy so do voting, speaking, and serving. Where the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what he commands, the line stands where the apostles and Daniel's friends drew it: refuse openly, without violence, and accept the cost.

Past that line, faithful Christians part ways, on questions that have divided churches without dividing the faith. Some hold that a believer may disobey only when commanded to sin; others, that he may openly break an unjust law and accept the penalty in order to expose it. The just-war tradition reads the sword of verse 4 as a calling a Christian may take up in a just cause, within strict limits; the peace churches read Romans 12 as the disciple's rule and verse 4 as what God does through the state. Whatever you conclude, conclude it before you know whose government it will bind.

Jesus stood before a governor who claimed the power to release or crucify him, and told him, “You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above” (John 19:11). He didn't call Pilate's authority false. He called it borrowed, let it do its worst, and was raised by the God who lent it. Every Christian posture toward the state passes through that courtroom. Honor the servant, and never mistake him for the master. That's hard under a government you fear, and harder under one you voted for.
